title: Time, days, and dates
title_target: 现在几点 — Xiànzài jǐ diǎn
goal: Tell the time, the day, the date, and the year; make plans; and master one ordering rule that runs through all of Mandarin — from big to small, and time always before the verb.
bekal: say the days of the week and the date
put time expressions in the right place
tell 号 from 日, and 星期 from 周

dialogs.title: 对话 1 — Making plans
dialogs.intro: Andi and Wang Li arrange a time to meet. Watch closely where each time expression stands — that's the whole lesson of this unit.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: What time is it now?
lines.literal: now — how-many — o'clock.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Half past three. What's up?
lines.literal: three — o'clock — half. how — (change).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [明天|Míngtiān][你|nǐ][有空|yǒu kòng][吗|ma]？[我|Wǒ][想|xiǎng][请|qǐng][你|nǐ][喝|hē][咖啡|kāfēi]。
lines.id: Are you free tomorrow? I'd like to buy you a coffee.
lines.literal: tomorrow — you — have-free-time — (question). I — would-like — treat — you — drink — coffee.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: What's the date tomorrow? What day?
lines.literal: tomorrow — how-many — date. week — how-many.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: May 12th, a Wednesday.
lines.literal: five — month — twelve — date, week — three.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [星期三|Xīngqīsān][上午|shàngwǔ][我|wǒ][有|yǒu][课|kè]，[下午|xiàwǔ][可以|kěyǐ]。
lines.id: I have class Wednesday morning, but the afternoon works.
lines.literal: week — three — upper-noon — I — have — class, lower-noon — may.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: How about three in the afternoon?
lines.literal: afternoon — three — o'clock — how-about.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Three's a bit early. Is four OK?
lines.literal: three — o'clock — a-bit — early. four — o'clock — OK — (question).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Sure! Let's meet at four at the school gate.
lines.literal: OK. we — four — o'clock — at — school — door-mouth — meet.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: OK. Don't be late!
lines.literal: good. don't — be-late — (ah).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Don't worry, I'm never late.
lines.literal: release — heart, I — ever — not — be-late.

notes: **⚠️ Time expressions stand BEFORE the verb, never after it.** [我三点去|Wǒ sān diǎn qù] = I'm going at three. 我去三点 is completely wrong. English puts the time at the end (“I'm going **at three**”); Mandarin puts it up front. This is the rule English speakers break most, and the one that decides whether your sentence sounds right.
**Time can also stand before the subject.** [明天我有课|Míngtiān wǒ yǒu kè] and [我明天有课|Wǒ míngtiān yǒu kè] are both correct. Only one place is **off-limits**: after the verb.

**[点|diǎn] = o'clock, [半|bàn] = half.** [三点半|sān diǎn bàn] means **half past three**, 3:30. ⚠️ The hour always comes first and 半 follows it — Mandarin never counts toward the next hour the way German *halb vier* (3:30) does.
**[几号|jǐ hào]？ what date; [星期几|xīngqī jǐ]？ what day.** Notice that 几 stands exactly where the answer goes: [五月十二号|wǔ yuè shí'èr hào], [星期三|xīngqīsān].
**[有空|yǒu kòng] = to be free, have time.** The opposite is [没空|méi kòng] or [很忙|hěn máng].
**[请|qǐng] has two meanings**: “please” ([请坐|qǐng zuò]) and “to treat, invite” ([我请你|wǒ qǐng nǐ] it's on me). At the dinner table, [我请客|wǒ qǐngkè] means “I'm paying”.
**[行|xíng] = “OK, fine”** — very colloquial, very common. [行吗|Xíng ma]？ is that OK? [行|Xíng]。 sure.
**[别|bié] + verb = don't.** [别迟到|Bié chídào] don't be late, [别走|bié zǒu] don't go. ⚠️ 不要 also means “don't” but sounds harsher.

grammars.title: Telling the time

head: Time
Mandarin
Note
rows: [三点零五分|sān diǎn líng wǔ fēn]
[三点四十五|sān diǎn sìshíwǔ] / [差一刻四点|chà yí kè sì diǎn]
[差十分四点|chà shí fēn sì diǎn]

after: The part of the day stands **before** the hour: [下午三点|xiàwǔ sān diǎn] 3 p.m., [晚上八点|wǎnshang bā diǎn] 8 p.m. Big first, small last — exactly like every Mandarin time expression.

grammars.title: Days, dates, months, years
body: Mandarin weekdays have no names of their own — they're numbered: [星期|xīngqī] + a number. The only exception is Sunday.

head: Unit
Spoken
Written
Example
rows: 2026 = [二零二六年|èr líng èr liù nián]

after: ⚠️ **Mandarin months are numbered too**: 一月 January, 二月 February, all the way to 十二月 December. No month names to memorize.
⚠️ **Years are read digit by digit**, not as a number. 2026 is [二零二六|èr líng èr liù], not “two thousand twenty-six”.

**Full date order: year → month → date → day → part of day → time.** 2026年5月12号星期三下午四点 — from biggest to smallest, without exception. English mostly runs the other way: “4 p.m., Wednesday, May 12, 2026”.

grammars.title: Common time expressions
after: ⚠️ Notice that [上|shàng] “up” means **last** and [下|xià] “down” means **next**. Chinese speakers picture time like a scroll read from top to bottom, not a line running to the right.
⚠️ Days break the pattern: **not** 上天/下天 but [昨天|zuótiān] and [明天|míngtiān]. Years do too: [去年|qùnián] and [明年|míngnián].

dialogs.title: 对话 2 — A daily routine
dialogs.intro: Li Ming talks about his days. Notice that every time expression comes before its action, without a single exception.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: What time do you get up every day?
lines.literal: you — every — day — how-many — o'clock — rise — bed.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Six thirty. Then I have breakfast at seven.
lines.literal: six — o'clock — half. then — seven — o'clock — eat — morning-meal.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: What time do you start work?
lines.literal: you — how-many — o'clock — go-to — shift.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Eight thirty. From eight thirty to five.
lines.literal: eight — o'clock — half. from — eight — o'clock — half — to — five — o'clock.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Where do you eat at lunchtime?
lines.literal: midday — you — at — where — eat — meal.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: In the company cafeteria. Cheap and fast.
lines.literal: at — company — cafeteria. cheap — also — fast.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: And at night? What time do you go to bed?
lines.literal: evening — (and)? you — how-many — o'clock — sleep — sleep.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Usually eleven. A bit later on weekends.
lines.literal: usually — eleven — o'clock. week-end — late — a-little.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: What do you do on weekends?
lines.literal: week-end — you — do — what.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.text: [星期六|Xīngqīliù][打球|dǎ qiú]，[星期天|xīngqītiān][在|zài][家|jiā][休息|xiūxi]。
lines.id: I play ball on Saturday and rest at home on Sunday.
lines.literal: week-six — play — ball, week-sky — at — home — rest.

notes: **[从…到…|cóng… dào…] = from … to ….** Used for time and place alike: [从八点到五点|cóng bā diǎn dào wǔ diǎn], [从家到公司|cóng jiā dào gōngsī].
**⚠️ [在|zài] + place also stands BEFORE the verb.** [我在食堂吃饭|Wǒ zài shítáng chī fàn] = I eat in the cafeteria. Not 我吃饭在食堂. Same rule as time: all the extra information comes before the action.
**[起床|qǐ chuáng], [吃饭|chī fàn], [上班|shàng bān], [睡觉|shuì jiào]** are all verb + object pairs that have fused together. Since the object is already inside, you can't add another object after them.
**[又…又…|yòu… yòu…] = “both … and …”.** [便宜又快|piányi yòu kuài] cheap and fast. The full form is [又便宜又快|yòu piányi yòu kuài].
**[一般|yìbān] = usually, generally.** A synonym is [通常|tōngcháng]. It goes before the verb, like every other time word.
**[周末|zhōumò] = weekend.** 周 is the written form of 星期, but 周末 is used in everyday speech too.

grammars.title: Sentence order — learn it once, use it forever
body: Here is the full frame of a Mandarin sentence. Once you've got it, you'll never wonder where to put extra information again.
after: Read the second row out loud word for word: “I tomorrow at home with friends watch a movie”. It sounds odd in English — and that's exactly what correct Mandarin sounds like.

⚠️ The only things that stand **after** the verb are the object and result complements. Time, place, and manner **never** go there. If you're unsure whether something can go at the end, the answer is almost always no.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: [你明天有空吗|Nǐ míngtiān yǒu kòng ma]？
[对不起，我有事|Duìbuqǐ, wǒ yǒu shì]。
[我可能会晚一点儿|Wǒ kěnéng huì wǎn yìdiǎnr]。
I might be a bit late.

blocks.title: Punctuality in China
items: For work and formal appointments, **on time means five minutes early**, not on the dot. Arriving at the exact minute already counts as cutting it close.
For a meal with friends, there's more leeway — but letting people know is still expected.
[我马上到|Wǒ mǎshàng dào] “I'll be right there” is used very loosely — much like “I'm on my way!” anywhere else.
⚠️ Canceling at the last minute is considered far ruder than being late. If you must, [改天吧|Gǎitiān ba] with a short reason is the safe form.

blocks.text: The Chinese calendar runs on two tracks: the solar calendar you know, and the traditional lunar calendar that sets the dates of festivals. That's why Chinese New Year falls on a different date every year.

head: Holiday
Mandarin
When
rows: Day 1 of lunar month 1 — January or February

blocks.title: Greetings and wishes
items: [新年快乐|Xīnnián kuàilè]！ — Happy New Year.
[恭喜发财|Gōngxǐ fācái]！ — “Wishing you prosperity” — the most common Chinese New Year greeting.
[生日快乐|Shēngrì kuàilè]！ — Happy birthday.
[祝你|Zhù nǐ]… — “Wishing you …” The opener for every good wish: [祝你身体健康|Zhù nǐ shēntǐ jiànkāng] wishing you good health.
⚠️ Never give a **clock** as a gift: [送钟|sòng zhōng] “give a clock” sounds exactly like [送终|sòng zhōng] “attend someone's deathbed”.
